blocks.content: The dns-resolution-flow topic walked through root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative servers in action, but treated the overall structure they belong to somewhat briefly. This topic zooms out and looks directly at that structure itself, the hierarchical tree that organizes every single domain name on the entire internet.

Understanding this tree shape makes the resolution flow from the previous topic feel obvious in hindsight, since the resolution process is really just walking down this exact tree, one level at a time.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015984343-973643531.png
blocks.alt: The DNS hierarchy: root at the top, then top level domains, then registered domains, then subdomains

blocks.content: 1. DNS Is Organized as a Tree
blocks.text: 1. DNS Is Organized as a Tree

blocks.content: Every domain name on the internet fits into one single, enormous tree structure. At the very top sits the root. Below the root sit the top level domains, .com, .org, .io, and many others. Below each top level domain sit the actual registered domains, like example.com. And below a registered domain, an organization is free to create as many subdomains as it wants, like www.example.com or api.example.com.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015986244-867912659.png
blocks.alt: A small piece of the DNS tree: root branching into top level domains, which branch into individually registered domains

blocks.content: 2. Reading a Domain Name Right to Left
blocks.text: 2. Reading a Domain Name Right to Left

blocks.content: This is a genuinely useful trick for understanding domain structure: a full domain name is actually read from RIGHT to LEFT to walk down the tree. Taking www.example.com apart this way: the implicit root, then com, the top level domain, then example, the specific registered domain, then www, a subdomain of that specific domain.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015987884-783554189.png
blocks.alt: Reading a domain name from right to left walks exactly down the tree, from root to top level domain to subdomain

blocks.content: 3. Root Servers: The Foundation

The root servers introduced in the resolution flow topic sit at the very top of this entire tree. There is a small, well known set of them, but each one is actually run across many physical machines distributed globally, using a technique that routes a request to the nearest available copy. This deliberate distribution makes them extremely reliable, with no single physical failure able to take the whole system down.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015989682-696139412.png
blocks.alt: Root servers are run across many distributed physical machines worldwide, deliberately avoiding any single point of failure

blocks.title: A genuinely critical piece of infrastructure
blocks.content: If the root servers were ever all unreachable at once, essentially no new DNS lookup starting from scratch could complete anywhere on the internet. Their reliability and distribution is treated with enormous seriousness for exactly this reason.
4. Types of Top Level Domains

Not all top level domains serve the same purpose. Generic top level domains, .com, .org, .net, are broadly available for general use. Country code top level domains, .uk, .in, .jp, are tied to specific countries. Sponsored top level domains, .edu, .gov, are restricted to specific kinds of organizations, universities and government bodies respectively.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015991291-989805881.png
blocks.alt: Top level domains come in several types: generic, country specific, and sponsored, restricted to certain organizations

5. Subdomains: Genuine Flexibility Within One Domain
blocks.text: 5. Subdomains: Genuine Flexibility Within One Domain

blocks.content: Once an organization registers a domain, it has complete freedom to create as many subdomains underneath it as it wants, with no need to register anything new or ask any outside authority for permission. www.example.com for the main website, api.example.com for a separate API service, mail.example.com for email, all live freely under the one single registered example.com domain.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015992930-923617320.png
blocks.alt: An organization can freely create as many subdomains as it wants under its own registered domain, with no outside approval needed

blocks.title: Subdomains cost nothing extra to create
blocks.content: Unlike registering a brand new domain, creating a new subdomain under a domain you already own requires no separate registration or fee at all, it is entirely under your own control.
6. A Postal System Analogy

A country postal system delegates responsibility in layers, exactly like DNS does. The country level delegates regional sorting down to states or provinces, which delegate local delivery down to individual cities, which finally delegate down to individual streets and addresses. Each layer only needs to understand its own local piece, trusting the layer above and below to handle the rest.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015994463-900264974.png
blocks.alt: A postal system delegating from country to state to city to street mirrors exactly how DNS delegates responsibility down its tree

blocks.content: 7. Decentralized Ownership Within a Centralized Structure
blocks.text: 7. Decentralized Ownership Within a Centralized Structure

blocks.content: The root and top level domain servers are managed by dedicated global authorities, following carefully coordinated rules. But once an organization actually registers a specific domain, it has genuine, complete autonomy to manage everything underneath that domain however it wants, entirely on its own. This balance, tight coordination at the top, real freedom underneath, is what lets DNS scale to the entire planet while still letting individual organizations manage their own piece freely.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015996046-252119576.png
blocks.alt: Tight coordination at the root and TLD level, combined with genuine autonomy for individual domain owners underneath
